catalog_quote: 2.2.1 STRESS. Stress, that is the prominence of one syllable as compared with neighbouring syllables by means of higher pressure of the airstream, is not contrastive in Meta'. It is, however, useful to distinguish between stressed and unstressed syllables, since certain tone rules can best be formulated by recourse to this distinction.[1] The initial syllable of each root has phonetic stress. All affix syllables and non-initial root syllables are unstressed. In the following examples stress is marked by ['] but will generally be left unmarked outside of this subsection. (1) (a) ə̀-ˈbàm ~ ə̀-ˈbàmɨ 'bag' (b) ə-ˈzéd ~ ə-ˈzérɨ 'tree, stick' (c) ˈnáb 'house, family' (d) ˈwə̀d 'person'. [fn 1: See §xxx for details] ... 2.2.2 THE TONAL SYSTEM. As a Western Grassfields Bantu language one expects Meta' to be highly tonal, and in fact phonetically four different levels of tone and six contour tones must be recognized. ... Meta' does not employ such a phenomenon, but has discrete levels of pitch with corresponding phonetic tones which are variants or combinations of three register tonemes.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Meta' is a tone language (three register tonemes, four phonetic levels plus six contours per the same source); stress is not contrastive. Phonetic stress falls on the initial syllable of the root; noun-class prefixes and other affixes and non-initial root syllables are unstressed. The stressed syllable is where long vowels can occur (Spreda 1991, 'Long vowels in Meta'' p. 1: 'Long vowels can only occur in stressed syllables. The stressed CV-syllables are generally roots of nouns and verbs.').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the distinction is said to be needed only for formulating certain tone rules (footnote 'See §xxx for details' — cross-reference never filled in in the draft).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: prefix + root nouns and verb roots cited in isolation (e.g. ə̀-'bàm 'bag', ə-'zéd 'tree'); the source is an unrevised 1995 SIL draft ('1st Rev'), posted 'as is'.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for Meta' proper (Spreda's 'Meta''/'Metta', ISO mgo, glottocode meta1238). Tunviken 2013, Njeck 2008 and Casali 1995 describe Moghamo, the divergent Batibo variety that Glottolog files under meta1238 (SIL's archive tags Tunviken's subject language as Ngamambo [nbv], but the text itself gives ISO mgo); those are tone-only and were not used for the stress reading. Spreda's 1995 draft is an SIL working manuscript posted without peer review, not a published grammar.

sources.citation: Spreda, Klaus W. (1997). Studies towards the segmental portion of an alphabet proposal for Moghamo. SIL Cameroon.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: This work describes Moghamo (Glottolog dialect mogh1246 of Meta' meta1238), compared throughout with Meta'; the Moghamo data are the sub-dialect of one speaker, John Mbo Ndam of Batibo. Meta' appears only as the comparison baseline (Meta' forms with tone marks, eight-vowel system, current Meta' orthography in the example sentences). The work presupposes a Meta' tone notation but states nothing about the tone or stress system, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's tone-and-stress class. It is a different work from the catalog's cited Spreda 1995 sketch-grammar draft.
